heldBackBy.answer: I think it was the secret potential ceiling (CEP) and the stuff I couldn't see, like STAND. INTEG and COMP were maxed out, but STAND stayed low because I kept speaking up and being honest on budgets. Maybe politics needs people to notice you more, and I never worked out how.
Honestly I don't think anything did, I got to DPM. Maybe the secret CEP ceiling capped me below PM, and the honesty choices cost me STAND along the way.

Honestly nothing, I got to Prime Minister. The only drag was STAND dipping every time I was honest, so being straight cost me a little each time but never blocked me. I'm not sure my choices mattered much since REP, INTEG and COMP were maxed early.

Mostly the STAND stat, which seemed to fall when I questioned the system or pressed for secrets, even when my work was outstanding. I think the game rewards going along with things, and my curiosity cost me.

I think it was being the honest, careful type. Asking about the ceiling, speaking up in Cabinet and choosing the proper, slow way kept my INTEG at 100 but kept my STAND low. The game rewards visibility and being safe more than being right.

Honestly, I kept asking awkward questions and being straight, which cost STAND again and again. I think the game punishes people who are too honest, so I never got the top job despite maxed INTEG, REP and COMP.

Probably the secret CEP ceiling, the hidden potential cap, not my integrity. I kept being honest and it kept paying, so I never got a real setback, and I still stopped at Minister without reaching the top.

Honestly I think nothing did. I played it straight, INTEG stayed at 100, and I still ended up DPM. Maybe the Y34 pay question and staying in an easy ministry stopped me going higher, but the game never said so.

I think being honest kept costing me STAND, and I never got on the Leadership Programme list. I always told the truth and asked awkward questions, so I was respected but not the one they picked for the top jobs.

My REP was too low because I kept choosing the honest, do-the-work, go-home options over being seen and networking. I think the game rewards visibility for the political route, and I never built it. The election result also seemed partly out of my hands.
My STAND stayed low because I kept answering straight and honestly, which the game seems to punish. I never got to the PM seat, probably because of that and the third column in the succession chart.
Mostly the Y38 Cabinet question on ministerial pay indicators, which cost 14 STAND, and the Y45 Facebook concession. Otherwise nothing really held me back, since I got to DPM anyway.

I think being honest and not playing politics cost me STAND, the thing that decides who gets to the top. Being the safe pair of hands means you never get picked as the leader. The dormant company and the Leadership Programme list leaving me out might also have been part of it, but the game never explained either.
My REP stat stayed at 50 the whole way, so I think being low-profile and not networking enough held me back. I was good at the work but not seen, and politics rewards being seen.
Honestly nothing much, I hit DPM. If anything, being too honest cost me a bit of STAND, and I never became PM, maybe because I backed the other candidate for succession.

Probably my STAND dropping every year from being too honest and not playing politics, but it never visibly cost me anything. I got to DPM and retired, so maybe nothing held me back except never becoming PM. I couldn't tell what the game wanted for that.

I think it was the secret ceiling grade (CEP), which I never saw or understood. Being honest also kept lowering my STAND, so I never got the quick promotions. I still made DPM, so I'm not sure what was really holding me back.

Me being too honest and asking awkward questions in front of seniors. INTEG stayed at 100 but STAND kept dropping, so the game seems to say being the one who says the thing out loud costs you the top job.
Probably me picking the honest or nice option every time. It cost STAND in the short term, and I only reached Minister at the end, at 72. Deferring the overseas posting in Y17 also quietly cost me.

My own honesty, I think. Every time I said the true thing, like the PQ answer or the Cabinet pay question, STAND dropped, and the CEP ceiling was set by people who didn't like that. I made it to Minister anyway, so the system seems to tolerate candour but not reward it.

My STAND with seniors kept sliding, probably from asking awkward questions like the Cabinet pay-indicator one in Y40, and from skipping clearance for my daughter's concert. I stayed honest, so I got REP and integrity but not the top jobs.

My guess is that STAND kept falling and I never worked out why, or the game just wanted me to stay a civil servant. Maybe the politics invite was never going to come, or that mystery nomination in Y28 was never explained. I really don't know.
Probably nothing much, I ended as DPM, one step short of PM, so maybe the unseen CEP capped me. My STAND kept sliding even when I was honest, so I think visibility mattered more than good work.

Being honest every time, and asking in Cabinet in Y38 if ministers should be paid on indicators they set. STAND crashed after that and colleagues marked me out. I think the game punishes people who rock the boat, and my CEP probably capped me anyway.

Being honest in public cost me STAND in the middle years, and I was left off the Leadership Programme list with no explanation. I think the system punishes people who say the quiet part out loud, then slowly rewards them if they last long enough. I got there at 70, which is late.

I think it was honesty. Every time I told the truth, like the Cabinet question or the Facebook concession, STAND dropped and never recovered. Maybe I was also never on the political track, since I kept getting MHA instead of the hard ministry I asked for.
Probably the secret CEP ceiling, the potential rating I couldn't see or change. Maybe also that I never played the politics game and kept choosing honesty over standing, so STAND stayed in the 50s.

Probably being too quiet and never pushing myself forward. The game kept hinting at a secret CEP rating and a ceiling I was never told about, so I think the system decided my potential early and nothing I did changed it much.
I think being a safe pair of hands and always answering honestly kept me out of the top job. The system liked me but never picked me for the Leadership Programme or PM, and I never got a reason why.

I think it was the secret ceiling, the CEP, plus me always picking the honest option. The system probably only lets you rise so far however clean you are. I also never learned how the game really works, so I stayed quiet and plain when I should have played it a bit.

I think being too honest cost me with the system, since STAND kept sliding even though REP and INTEG stayed at 100. Never padding or spinning meant I got promoted but never became the favourite. Honestly, I still don't fully get what STAND measures.

I think being straight and honest cost me STAND, so the system seems to reward playing safe more than being correct. I topped out as Minister but never felt like I was getting ahead, and I never really understood what the grades meant.
I think I was too safe. HR called me a 'safe pair of hands', which probably means they park you there. I never took a real risk, so I stopped at DPM and never became PM.

I think being too straight and always picking honesty over looking good meant I never got the shiny stuff like Harvard or the top job. The Y23 question to Cabinet and the Y28 ask for a hard ministry probably cost me more than anything.

I don't think anything held me back, because I ended up as PM. The only thing that lagged was STAND, which kept sagging even when I did the honest thing. Maybe the game is saying honesty makes you less popular but gets you paid.

My honesty about the system, like unflattering PQ answers and asking whether ministers should be paid on indicators they set, probably kept me off the top job and the Leadership list. But I still reached DPM, so it looks like it cost me one rung, not everything.

Low REP at 51, I think. I never really knew how to raise it, and I picked things on instinct that felt nice, not things that built my public profile. The game also said the loss was never about me, which is fair but a bit frustrating.
Honestly nothing really held me back, I became PM at 59 with integrity 100. The only dip was STAND at 66, from being honest in public, but it didn't stop anything.

Honestly nothing much, I got to DPM. If anything it was the succession chart thing where my name stayed in the third column, so maybe the game wanted me to be a bit more political or less safe. The Yr10 and Yr5 going home early probably cost a bit of appraisal.

Probably my honesty costing STAND each time, plus those two public-reply choices in the succession race. I still made PM, so I don't think anything really held me back. The game seems to reward steady, boring good behaviour.
Honestly nothing much, I got to PM with integrity 100. Maybe my standing dipping from being candid, but it never stopped me climbing.
Honestly, I don't think I was held back. I became PM at 59 with integrity 100. The only cost was STAND, which kept dropping because I kept answering straight.
I think being too honest, especially the Cabinet question about ministers' pay in Y43. The game seems to punish honesty once you get near the top, and STAND never recovered after that.
Not much, I made PM at 59 with integrity 100. If anything the straight PQ answers kept my STAND lower in the later years, so honesty cost me popularity but not the top job.
My STAND kept dropping because I always picked the honest, straight answer, so I never got to PM. I stopped at DPM, probably because I wasn't popular or political enough.
Honestly I don't think anything held me back, since I ended up PM at 59. The only drag was STAND falling every time I answered honestly, so being straight costs popularity but doesn't block the job.
Mostly the STAND stat. I kept choosing honest, listening options that cost popularity, and I think that is the game's quiet trade-off. Still, I became PM, so nothing really held me back.

My own honesty, mostly. Every time I answered straight or admitted something, my standing with colleagues dropped, even though integrity stayed at 100. I never really got punished for anything except being the awkward one.
Honestly I don't think anything did, since I ended up PM. If anything it was the honest answers dragging STAND down, but that never stopped the promotions, so it didn't feel like they mattered.

toneBreaks.line: You served. The service continued. Both of these facts are entirely unremarkable and that is the highest compliment the system can pay.
toneBreaks.note: A bit smug and self-aware, like the game is congratulating itself on being dry. It's fine but it did wink.

toneBreaks.line: You served. The service continued. Both of these facts are entirely unremarkable and that is the highest compliment the system can pay.
toneBreaks.note: Clever line but it winks at the reader a bit. It reads like the game patting itself on the back, though I did kind of like it.

toneBreaks.line: HR called me 'a safe pair of hands'
toneBreaks.note: Not a break, but the CEP and grade jargon around it lost me. I didn't know the grades and the game never explained them.

toneBreaks.line: Y2 Director asked if the system is a joke, then winked
toneBreaks.note: The wink was never explained and never came back, so it just felt like the game teasing me.

toneBreaks.line: Y8: 'Is the system a joke, a game?'
toneBreaks.note: Funny, but the Director's wink felt a bit knowing, as if the game was commenting on itself.

toneBreaks.line: Pay header ($32.93M) vs annual package (~$2.5M)
toneBreaks.note: Not a tone break but I never understood why the two numbers differ, and it made the money feel unreliable.

toneBreaks.line: You served. The service continued. Both of these facts are entirely unremarkable and that is the highest compliment the system can pay.
toneBreaks.note: Slightly smug, like the game is congratulating itself. Not a big deal.

toneBreaks.line: Pay shown as $39.97M versus $2.5M package
toneBreaks.note: I could not tell what the numbers meant, and the final card said $42.5M lifetime, which made it more confusing.

toneBreaks.line: You served. The service continued. Both of these facts are entirely unremarkable

best.what: Fought for my people's postings and it led to a promotion. It was one of the few times a choice paid off in a way I could see.

worst.what: Year Without Incident again, building a network because the boss wanted me 'more visible' to unspecified people. Vague, and nothing came of it.

skip.why: Quiet fix nobody asked for. It cost STAND and gave nothing back. Those 'Year Without Incident' years felt like filler.

diaries.fair: Perm Sec at the top of the service with 100 integrity is a decent result. It felt a bit flat, but I did pick the honest options every time, so I can't complain.
diaries.again: It's a long run to repeat. Too many similar years in the middle, and I'd want a break before going back for another 40 years of taps.

best.what: Listening to the chilli stallholder on camera, and then having him pop up again in Y32 and Y46. A small human moment that kept coming back.

worst.what: The mid-career stretch of civil service grade years, where it was all acronyms and appraisal boxes I didn't understand and I just tapped through.

skip.why: Skipping clearance for my daughter's concert felt like a nothing choice, and I never saw it really matter after that.

diaries.fair: Retiring as DPM with 100 integrity fits how I played, honest and steady. It felt a bit flat but not unfair.
diaries.again: A full run is about 49 taps and lots of it blurred together. I'd come back later for the PM ending, but not tonight.

best.what: Wrote the appeal letters properly for the man whose case couldn't be reopened, after he came back from the Y25 appeal letters thing. That callback felt like the game remembered me.

worst.what: Another PQ with an unflattering answer, same honest-answer, STAND dips then recovers loop as the year before and after. By then it felt like tapping the same button.

skip.why: Townhall with the impolite workload question was a repeat of earlier townhall and PQ years. I knew the outcome before I tapped, and nothing new landed.

diaries.fair: I played honest and steady and got the top job, so it felt earned. But it also felt a bit inevitable because the stats were maxed so long, and the ending card was short on what the career meant. The pay line about the published formula was a nice jab.
diaries.again: A whole life is a lot of taps and the last stretch was repetitive, so I'd want a break first. I'd come back for a different path, but not right now.

best.what: The man from Meet-the-People came back and 3 of my 11 appeal letters had worked. It was the one time a small choice paid off in a way I could actually see.

worst.what: I asked a reasonable question in Cabinet about indicator-based pay and STAND dropped 14 with no clear explanation, even though my appraisal stayed outstanding. It felt like the game punishing me for no reason I could follow.

skip.why: By then it was the third townhall workload question and I picked A every time. It felt like filler with no new information.

diaries.fair: I got to PM with integrity at 100 and the line about the published formula was a good wry closer. I did wonder what I could have done differently, but I got there honestly.
diaries.again: It was a long run on my phone in bed and I did the same kind of choices a lot. I'd come back another day, but not right now.

best.what: Became MP and the chilli stallholder clip went viral. It was the first time the game felt funny and human, and I actually wanted to see what happened next.

worst.what: Learning about CEP, the secret ceiling grade. It was an acronym dump and I didn't really get it. The explanation felt like reading an HR memo, and asking about it hurt my STAND for no reason I could see.

skip.why: Quiet year where I fixed something nobody asked for. Nothing happened and nothing came back, so it was just a tap before the ending.

diaries.fair: Fair enough. I got a clean 100 integrity and made Minister, and 'a safe pair of hands' summed up how I played. It was a bit flat, though. I expected something to pay off, like the contractor cousin or the pay indicators, and it just said I retired.
diaries.again: It's a long run and a lot of years felt similar. I'd come back another day for the cheeky-career run, but not right now in bed.

best.what: Reporting the real utilisation numbers and getting promoted to AD the next year, the first time honesty paid off and made me want to keep going.

worst.what: The Parliamentary Question and the later years of walkabouts and townhalls felt samey, with the same choice of answering straight and the same small STAND nudge.

skip.why: The wet market walkabout was just another listen-to-the-public tap with nothing new, and I could have skipped it without missing anything.

diaries.fair: Fair enough. I stayed clean and rose to Minister, so retiring quietly at 72 fits. Slightly flat as an ending, but it matches how I played.
diaries.again: It was fun at the start, but I could see the pattern by the end and the later years felt repetitive. Maybe in a few days, once I've forgotten the loop.

best.what: Nominated the quiet officer over myself, and she later became Deputy Secretary and named me for the last rung. That felt like a proper payoff for a choice I made on instinct.

worst.what: Another townhall, another rude question read out. By then it felt like the same choice repeated, and the pay numbers on screen were just a blur I didn't follow.

skip.why: The MPS year with 41 residents and appeal letters was a lot of reading. I was waiting for the weekly man's case to come back and the game ended before it did.

diaries.fair: I stayed honest the whole way and ended as a Minister with Integrity 100, so retiring quietly and respectably fits. I did want a bit more drama after that many years, though.
diaries.again: It was fun in short bursts, but I've just done 40-plus years of tapping and I'm done for tonight. I'd come back another day, maybe.

best.what: The Director asked if the system is 'a joke, a game', I stayed silent and she winked. It was the one moment that felt like a proper human beat.

worst.what: The MPS man returning every Tuesday and the appeal letters grind. Repetitive, and 3 of 11 succeeding felt like admin, not a story.

skip.why: The start of the MPS Tuesday loop. Quiet years kept repeating the same menu and nothing changed for me.

diaries.fair: Retiring honourably with integrity 100 matches how I played. It was a bit flat, but it fit. I only wish the game had told me more about why I stopped at Minister.
diaries.again: It was long and I always picked the same type of choice. I'd need a reason to be someone different, and right now I'm done for tonight.

best.what: The chilli stallholder kept getting listened to on camera. A small recurring thing that felt human and a bit funny, and it kept coming back.

worst.what: Asking in Cabinet if ministers should be paid on indicators they set. It felt like the game was lecturing me, and STAND just dropped with no real payoff.

skip.why: Another townhall with the same rude workload question. By then it was the same tap I'd done fifteen times and nothing new happened.

diaries.fair: I played honest and steady and got a clean DPM retirement, which matches. But a few threads never paid off: the Director test, the BTO result, the dormant company and the Forum fallout. So it felt a bit unfinished.
diaries.again: 49 years of taps is a lot for one sitting and I've seen the clean path. I'd come back another day to try being sneaky, not right now.

best.what: Listening to the chilli stallholder at the walkabout and it going viral. Felt human and funny, and it came back again in Y48.

worst.what: The post-it fallout. I didn't get the civil service politics, and it felt like admin stuff I was reading just to get past it.
